pass_b_english: We will entrust our praise and hymns to the one who alone can heal our weakness and supply what we lack, the ruler and savior of our souls, the firstborn Word, the creator and ruler of all, who stands above all and over all. Through him we are able to send continuous, unceasing thanks to the Father, because he is the truth, the wisdom, and the power of the Father of all. He is in the Father and with the Father, inseparably united, so that it is impossible to approach the Father except through him, or to praise the Father except through the power of praise, or to reach the Father except through the power of praise. He alone is able to fulfill perfectly the worth of the praise due to him. The Father has made him one with himself, and through him the Son has made himself worthy of honor and praise above all and alone, possessing all the Father's power as the only-begotten Son in whom God the Word dwells. We are able to be thankful and pious only through him, if we offer to him alone, in place of all the good things we receive from the Father, the power of worthy thanksgiving, acknowledging this to be the one way of piety — the remembrance of the cause of all things through him.

Therefore, since he exercises providence over all, caring for us in the greatest and the least matters, he is worthy to be the logos of thanksgiving and hymns, perfect and living, and the first logos himself is living. Our own thanksgiving is directed toward this holy man, especially toward the one who has been a benefactor to me. If I wanted to speak further, I would also include the invisible, more divine beings, toward this one who was appointed by a great judgment to manage, entrust, and oversee me — a holy angel of God who has nourished me from my youth, as that friend of God says, referring to himself. But I do not know clearly whether this great one is another, or perhaps even the angel of the great counsel himself, the common savior of all, who has been appointed solely as guardian of perfection. I do know, however, that he knows and praises his own great one. We give thanks to the common ruler and savior of all men, who is also our pedagogue. He nourishes and cares for me, not because I or my friends deserve it — for we are blind and see nothing before us, so we cannot judge what is needed — but because he, foreseeing all that benefits our souls, makes it appear profitable. Long ago and even now, among all his other works, he has joined me to this man — the most decisive thing of all — though he was not related to me by birth or human blood, nor did he live nearby or share my race, the usual grounds for friendship among most people. Rather, he brought together strangers, aliens, those utterly separated from each other, divided by many nations, mountains, and rivers, and through truly divine and wise providence he engineered this saving meeting for me. I think he has been providing for this from my very first birth and upbringing. How it happened I cannot trace in detail, nor would I pretend to be exact and omit nothing. But if I chose to pass over much and briefly recall only a few of the most important points, I could.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the complex theological structure of the Greek text, including the relationship between the Father and the Word. Pass A preserves the nuances of the Greek clauses, and Pass B provides a fluent, accurate rendering that does not contradict the source. All specific theological distinctions (e.g., the role of the Word as the 'logos of thanksgiving') are maintained.
